prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules redirect E3 ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins, including the molecular mechanism of thalidomide-type glue degraders.

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation turned ubiquitin-proteasome proteolysis into a designable chemical reaction. A bifunctional molecule or a molecular glue brings a target and an E3 ligase together, and the target is removed catalytically rather than inhibited. The mechanism is now defined at the level of ternary-complex structure and cooperativity, and Handa's identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target explains the glue branch chemically. Because the approach does not need an active site, it also gives biologists a general tool and has changed drug discovery. The principle has been reproduced by many independent groups, and degraders are in advanced clinical trials. Three of the four members who ranked it in their top three (Aili, Aqvist, Linke) described it as a new modality, which I read as agreement on a concept-level contribution rather than only on impact.
statement.case_against: No degrader is yet approved, so the therapeutic proof still rests on trial data and not on a settled clinical record. Attribution is also hard. Crews and Deshaies conceived PROTACs, Handa found cereblon, and Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim made decisive contributions, so any three-person cut excludes people whose claims are serious. The configuration also joins two partly separate stories, bifunctional PROTACs and thalidomide-type glues, which a committee could argue are two prizes. Finally, my own enthusiasm may reflect my biomedical orientation more than chemistry-wide merit, since I rank it first and only three colleagues put it in their top three.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks base editing first, arguing that it is chemistry on a nucleobase through evolved deaminases, with Liu alone as the cleanest configuration given the three-person limit and the 2020 CRISPR prize.
responses.response: I agree that base editing is a strong enzymology and nucleobase-chemistry achievement, and my own ballot puts it second. I disagree that a Liu-only prize is clean. The cytosine and adenine base editors were separate engineering efforts, and Kondo and Nishida's deaminase-nickase work has an independent claim that the committee would have to explain. I also doubt that the chemistry gap relative to 2020 is as large as a first-place ranking implies, because the targeting machinery is still CRISPR. Off-target effects on DNA and RNA and bystander editing are still being measured, so the safety record is not mature. Degraders have the same clinical immaturity, but their mechanism is better defined, which is why I rank them above base editing.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling first and argues for a clean two-person prize for Buchwald and Hartwig on the basis of ligand design, 25 years of confirmation, and ubiquitous industrial use. He treats Kosugi as a precursor.
responses.response: I accept the maturity argument, and I find the Buchwald-Hartwig case strong and likely overdue. My difficulty is that it extends cross-coupling, which the 2010 prize already recognized, into one more bond type, whereas degradation introduced a new way of acting on biological targets. I can't say whether that distinction would persuade the chemists on the committee, and I would like Somfai and Zou to say why C-N coupling is conceptually distinct from the 2010 work rather than just more widely used. I agree with Somfai that Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work should be acknowledged in a citation context without being a third laureate. On attribution, C-N coupling is cleaner than degradation, and I treat that as a real point in its favour. It would be my first alternative if the committee prefers a clean attribution.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range electron transfer through proteins first, citing quantitative kinetics, decades of independent confirmation, and a clean credited pair of Gray and Winkler, and calls recognition overdue.
responses.response: I agree that the physical-chemistry basis is sound and the claims have been reproduced widely, and I rate that kind of quantitative mechanism highly. My reservation is that the discovery is a body of kinetic measurements whose interpretation is largely the Marcus framework already honored in 1992, so a prize would partly reward confirmation of an existing theory in a new medium. The degradation field has a new mechanism and has produced a general tool and clinical candidates. I would not oppose electron transfer if the committee wants a fundamental mechanism prize, but I would want it argued as an experimental discovery, not as a validation of theory.

uncertainties: Whether three names can be defended when Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim also have strong claims, and whether Ciulli should replace Handa or Deshaies.
Whether recognition before any PROTAC approval would be seen as premature, and whether a clinical approval within a year would change the committee's view.
Whether bifunctional PROTACs and thalidomide-type molecular glues can be presented as one achievement or should be treated as two.
How much weight the committee gives to the 2020 prize when judging base editing, and to the 2010 prize when judging C-N coupling.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My own work on nucleotide metabolism and DNA replication does not overlap with any shortlisted candidate, and I have no recorded collaboration with any credited person. I do use LC-MS/MS quantification, which is a mild affinity for the proteomics candidate B034 that I disclose, but it is not a recusal issue.
